newsitem.title: Australia: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: TRADE SANCTIONS AGAINST BURMA NOT APPROPRIATE-GOVT
The Federal Government says it's not appropriate to impose trade sanctions on Burma.

A spokesman for Foreign minister Alexander Downer says Australia continues to call on the SLORC to enter into meaningful dialogue with Aung San Suu Kyi in order to return Burma to democratic government.

The spokesman says Australia has already introduced restrictions on dealing with the SLORC regime, including a policy of neither encouraging nor discouraging trade with Burma. The spokesman says unlike the United States, Australia has a very low level of investment and trade with Burma.
Mr Downer's office says for sanctions to be effective, they would have to be universal.
PASTORALISTS IN CANBERRA TO LOBBY ON NATIVE TITLE
A delegation of Northern Territory pastoralists is in Canberra to lobby the Federal Government on native title and pastoral leases.
Mr Howard will put the Government's final proposal to a special meeting of State and Territory leaders in Canberra on Monday, and then to Federal Cabinet later in the day.

President of the Northern Territory's Cattlemen's Association, David Bayly, says Territory pastoralists have reached agreements with Aboriginal people but they're being adversely affected through interference by outside parties, especially indigenous representative bodies.
He says pastoralists have had difficulties over ownership and use of stock routes, stock yards and water, and the Govenrment needs to understand that regional agreements are not working.
BEAZLEY OPPOSES CHANGES TO CROSS MEDIA OWNERSHIP RULES
The Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, says Kerry Packer's proposal to take over the Fairfax group should not be allowed while he still controls Channel Nine.
Mr Beazley says he has no problem with the Fairfax group being owned by one person, but diversity is eliminated when that person also owns or controls a television network.
Mr Beazley says he'll ensure the ALP's opposition to changes to cross media ownership rules is heard, even though it can't block the move in the Senate.
HANSON SHOWS STRAIN OF CANNIBALISM CLAIM
Federal Independent MP Pauline Hanson has shown the strain of dealing with claims in her book that Aborigines were once cannibals.
The cannibalism claims in the book "Pauline Hanson - The Truth", have been widely criticised by Australian historians.
Ms Hanson became emotional when she told a packed meeting at Gatton west of Brisbane last night that she'd had a tough day dealing with the controversy.
Australian Reform Party Director and meeting organiser, Alan Spencer, says Ms Hanson pointed out that the material on cannibalism was researched by other people, and was not written by her.
BOEING 727 RETIRES
The plane that is said to have "shrunk Australia" will have its last domestic flight today.
Ansett is selling its fleet of Boeing 727's, which when introduced in 1964, made air travel viable for most people, due to its reduced costs and higher speeds.
The 727, which made remote areas of Australia more accessible, will take passengers to Melbourne Airport for the last time this afternoon.
HOWARD WILL OVERTURN WIK DECISION SAYS BORBIDGE
Queensland Premier, Rob Borbidge, says the Prime Minister is prepared to amend the Racial Discrimination Act to overturn the High Court's Wik Decision.
Mr Borbidge says Mr Howard has indicated to all the premiers previously that he's prepared to consider winding back the Act.
Mr Borbidge says if changes to the Racial Discrimination Act are necessary to extinguish native title on pastoral leases, then so be it.
He says it's just another piece of legislation and the nation expects decisive action from the Prime Minister on the issue of native title.
GUN LOBBY DENIES DUNBLANE FATHER ABUSED TINGLE
The Coalition for Gun Control denies claims that a visiting Dublane father abused Shooters' Party MP John Tingle in the foyer of the New South Wales Parliament yesterday.
Mr Tingle alleges he was approached by one of the three fathers whose children were killed or wounded in last year's Dublane massacre in Scotland.
He claims the man criticised his views on guns, called him a murderer and thrust a picture of his daughter in his face.
Mr Tingle blames the anti-gun lobby who sponsored the visit, which coincides with the anniversary of the Port Arthur massacre.
But gun control campaigner Rebecca Peters says Mr Tingle's misrepresenting the conversation with the father and trying to draw attention to himself in a bizarre way.
